transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Please don't keep resetting the trip. Leave the appliance unplugged and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer before using it again. An induction hob that intermittently takes out the house electrics is most likely developing an electrical leakage fault. On an induction hob, the usual suspects are the power module or coil wiring; moisture beneath the glass after a spill/clean, or a poor mains connection, can do the same. Please do not use the hob again until it has been checked by a qualified appliance engineer or electrician. 1. Check the ceramic glass, surrounding worktop and cupboard below for signs of a recent spill, cleaner getting into an edge, scorching, discolouration or a hot-plastic smell. Moisture points towards drying/ingress; scorching or smell points towards a connection or power-component fault.
2. Note what has tripped at the consumer unit: the RCD/main safety switch, or the hob circuit breaker. Also note whether it coincides with one particular zone or high power setting. That helps the engineer distinguish a zone power section from supply wiring. If there is any burning smell, scorch mark or heat at the isolator switch, leave it isolated and arrange an electrician urgently.

ok, I'll leave it alone. There was a faint electrical smell once after it tripped. It's a big switch in the middle of the fuse box that drops, I don't know what it's called. There were a couple of boil-overs too.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. The large switch in the middle is very likely the RCD/main residual-current safety switch. Its job is to cut power when it detects electricity leaking to earth, so this is not a normal overload. The boil-overs make moisture getting beneath the glass a plausible contributor, but the faint electrical smell means an internal induction power module, coil wiring or connection may also be overheating or leaking. It must stay isolated and be checked by a qualified appliance engineer or electrician; drying it out is not a reason to put it back into use. With it switched off and isolated, only inspect externally: look around the glass edges, controls, underside cupboard and wall isolator for staining, residue, scorching or any heat damage. Any scorching, melted plastic or burnt smell at the isolator means use an electrician urgently. An engineer will need to inspect the supply connection and carry out insulation testing, then check the induction power electronics and coil wiring. Do not remove the hob or its covers, and do not keep resetting the RCD to test it.

candidates: Induction power module, coil or associated wiring developing an earth-leakage fault (high)
Moisture from a spill or cleaning product tracking beneath the glass (medium)
Loose or heat-damaged mains connection at the hob or isolator (medium)

plan: Safety: a supply trip hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
Already given by the customer, never ask for it again: make Hisense.
The fault they reported is: "house electrics go off intermittently when using the hob". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
